missions/church-missionary-society/name: Church Missionary Society (1799: Venn's three-self principle, Crowther, East Africa)
missions/church-missionary-society/origi: Castle and Falcon inn, Aldersgate Street, London
missions/church-missionary-society/statu: Renamed the Church Mission Society in 1995 and recognised as an Acknowledged Community of the Church of England in 2008, CMS continues to send and support mission workers and trains pioneer ministers. Its former fields are self-governing Anglican provinces, including the Church of Nigeria, the Church of Uganda and the Anglican Church of Kenya, which together make up a large share of the Anglican Communion's active membership and have become leading voices in it.
missions/church-missionary-society/summa: The evangelical Anglican mission society founded in London on 12 April 1799 by members of the Eclectic Society and the Clapham circle. Beginning with German Lutheran missionaries in Sierra Leone, it became the largest British missionary society of the nineteenth century, working in West and East Africa, India, New Zealand, Canada, China, Japan and the Middle East. Under Henry Venn it articulated the 'three-self' goal of self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending churches and consecrated Samuel Ajayi Crowther as the first African Anglican bishop (1864), though a later generation of missionaries undermined him. CMS-founded churches in Nigeria, Uganda and Kenya are now among the largest in the Anglican Communion.
missions/church-missionary-society/story:
Evangelical Anglicans of the Eclectic Society, among them John Venn of Clapham, Charles Simeon, John Newton, Henry Thornton and William Wilberforce, wanted a mission society that, unlike the non-denominational London Missionary Society, was faithful to the Church of England, but which, unlike the older SPG, was run by evangelicals. On 12 April 1799 they founded the Society for Missions to Africa and the East at the Castle and Falcon inn in Aldersgate Street; it took the name Church Missionary Society in 1812. Thomas Scott was its first secretary and Josiah Pratt its organiser. Because no English clergy volunteered at first, its first missionaries were German Lutherans trained at Johann Jänicke's Berlin seminary, Melchior Renner and Peter Hartwig, who sailed for Sierra Leone in 1804.

Sierra Leone became the society's first great field. After Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807, Royal Navy patrols landed tens of thousands of 'recaptives' liberated from slave ships at Freetown, and CMS missionaries such as W. A. B. Johnson at Regent (1816–23) gathered them into Christian villages. Fourah Bay Institution (1827), later affiliated to Durham University (1876), produced an educated West African clergy. Its first student was Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Yoruba boy enslaved in 1821, freed by the Royal Navy in 1822 and baptised in 1825. Crowther joined the Niger Expedition of 1841, was ordained in London in 1843, translated the Bible into Yoruba, went to Abeokuta with Henry Townsend in 1846, and from 1857 led an all-African Niger Mission. Meanwhile CMS also entered New Zealand, where Samuel Marsden preached the first sermon on Christmas Day 1814 at Oihi in the Bay of Islands; Henry Williams later translated the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) into Māori, a translation whose differences from the English text remain at the centre of debate about Māori sovereignty.

Henry Venn, honorary secretary from 1841 to 1872, gave the society its theory of mission. In papers of 1851, 1855 and 1861 he argued that missions should aim at the 'euthanasia of a mission': the creation of native churches that were self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending, under native pastors and eventually native bishops, after which the missionaries would move on. In 1864, at Venn's urging, Crowther was consecrated in Canterbury Cathedral as bishop of 'the countries of Western Africa beyond the limits of the Queen's dominions'. In India CMS worked from Agra (where Abdul Masih, a convert of Henry Martyn, served from 1813), in Tirunelveli (where Rhenius and others built a mass movement among Nadars), in Travancore (a 'Mission of Help' to the Syrian Christians from 1816, which ended in a split in 1836 and ultimately in the Mar Thoma reform movement), and in the Punjab and on the North-West Frontier from 1852. Thomas Valpy French founded St John's College, Agra (1850), and became first bishop of Lahore (1877).

In East Africa the German CMS missionaries Johann Ludwig Krapf (who arrived at Mombasa in 1844, after earlier work in Ethiopia, and lost his wife and baby within weeks) and Johannes Rebmann settled at Rabai; Rebmann was the first European to report Kilimanjaro (1848) and Krapf Mount Kenya (1849). Frere Town (1875) near Mombasa received freed slaves. After H. M. Stanley's 1875 appeal from the court of Kabaka Mutesa I of Buganda, a CMS party reached the kingdom in 1877, followed in 1878 by the engineer Alexander Mackay. Under Kabaka Mwanga Christian converts were persecuted: Bishop James Hannington was killed in Busoga in October 1885, and in 1885–87 dozens of Anglican and Catholic pages and officials were executed, the Uganda Martyrs. After civil wars between Protestant, Catholic and Muslim factions (1888–92), CMS supporters lobbied the British government to retain Uganda, which became a protectorate in 1894; the Anglican chiefs led by Apolo Kagwa dominated the kingdom, and Baganda evangelists such as Apolo Kivebulaya carried Christianity to Toro and the Congo.

The 1880s brought a crisis in the Niger Mission. Young, Keswick-influenced English missionaries, among them G. W. Brooke and J. A. Robinson, accused Crowther's African clergy of laxity and took control of the mission's finances in 1890; Crowther died in 1891 and was succeeded by a European bishop. The affair, which historians including J. F. Ade Ajayi, Andrew Walls and Jehu Hanciles treat as a turning point, discredited Venn's policy for a generation and contributed to the formation of African-led churches such as the United Native African Church (1891) and the Niger Delta Pastorate under James Johnson. In the same era CMS grew dramatically through university recruits inspired by the 'Cambridge Seven' and Keswick, entering Japan (1869), Persia (1869), China (Ningbo 1848, Fujian 1850, where eleven CMS and CEZMS missionaries and children were killed at Kucheng in 1895) and Canada's Rupert's Land, where it had worked since 1822 and ordained Henry Budd, the first Indigenous Anglican priest in North America, in 1850.

In the twentieth century CMS-related churches in Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda were transformed by the East African Revival (from 1929–35, among CMS missionaries such as Joe Church and Africans such as Simeon Nsibambi), while CMS clashed with Kikuyu leaders over female circumcision (1929–31) and later navigated Mau Mau. Under Max Warren (general secretary 1942–63) CMS became a thoughtful voice on mission after empire. The provinces it helped create became autonomous, among them Nigeria (1979), Uganda (1961) and Kenya (1970), and Nigerian, Ugandan and Kenyan Anglicans have since become numerically and theologically prominent in the Anglican Communion, notably in GAFCON. The society itself, renamed the Church Mission Society in 1995, now presents mission as a two-way relationship and sends mission partners from and to every continent.
missions/church-missionary-society/belie: Evangelical Anglicanism: the authority of Scripture, justification by faith, the necessity of conversion, the Book of Common Prayer and the Thirty-Nine Articles.
Loyalty to the episcopal order of the Church of England, with mission conducted by a voluntary society within the church rather than by the hierarchy.
Venn's 'three-self' principle: missions should create self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending native churches and then withdraw ('the euthanasia of a mission').
Opposition to the slave trade and slavery, inherited from the Clapham Sect, and a belief in 'legitimate commerce' and education as the alternative.
In the later nineteenth century, Keswick holiness spirituality and premillennial urgency shaped many recruits.
missions/church-missionary-society/strat: Settlements and schools for liberated Africans and freed slaves (Freetown villages, Frere Town).
Training indigenous clergy and teachers: Fourah Bay College (1827), CMS College Kottayam (1815), St John's College Agra (1850), Bishop Tucker College Mukono (1913).
Vernacular translation: Yoruba (Crowther), Igbo, Luganda, Swahili (Krapf), Māori, Malayalam (Benjamin Bailey) and other languages.
Appointing indigenous bishops and pastorates under Venn, beginning with Crowther (1864) and the Sierra Leone Native Pastorate (1861).
Medical missions such as Mengo Hospital in Kampala (1897, Albert Cook) and hospitals in Amritsar, Peshawar and Multan.
Political lobbying in Britain, as in the campaign to retain Uganda (1892) and in anti-slavery causes.
Women's missionary work through CMS women missionaries and allied societies such as the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society.
missions/church-missionary-society/group: Liberated Africans (recaptives) of many origins in Sierra Leone, and Krio society.
Yoruba, Igbo, Ijaw and other peoples of southern Nigeria and the Niger Delta.
Baganda, Basoga, Banyoro, Batoro and other peoples of Uganda; Kikuyu, Luo and Mijikenda in Kenya; Rwandans, Burundians and Tanzanians.
Nadars and Dalits in Tirunelveli, Syrian Christians and Dalits in Travancore, and urban and Punjabi communities in North India and Pakistan.
Cree and other First Nations in Rupert's Land and British Columbia; Chinese in Fujian and Zhejiang; Japanese, Persians, Egyptians and Palestinians.
missions/church-missionary-society/chall: A shortage of English clergy in the early decades, making the society dependent on German Lutheran missionaries.
Very high mortality in West Africa: dozens of CMS missionaries died in Sierra Leone in the society's first two decades.
Tension with bishops and high-church Anglicans over the society's evangelical independence.
Political violence: persecution in Buganda (1885–87), religious civil wars there (1888–92), the Kucheng massacre in China (1895).
Resistance from Hindu, Muslim and Buddhist communities and very slow growth among Muslims in North India, Persia and Egypt.
Racial tension between missionaries and African and Asian clergy, culminating in the Niger crisis of 1887–91.
missions/church-missionary-society/harms: The humiliation of Bishop Crowther and his African clergy by young European missionaries (1887–91), and the appointment of white successors, set back African church leadership for half a century.
CMS lobbying helped secure British imperial rule over Uganda, and Anglican chiefs used the protectorate to entrench Protestant political dominance.
In New Zealand missionaries' land purchases and the ambiguous Māori translation of the Treaty of Waitangi contributed to Māori dispossession.
CMS-founded schools for First Nations children in Canada fed into the residential school system, now recognised as gravely harmful.
Missionary campaigns against female circumcision in Kenya (1929–31) were pursued with expulsions from church and school that alienated many Kikuyu.
The Travancore 'Mission of Help' to the Syrian Christians ended in mutual recrimination and schism in 1836.
missions/church-missionary-society/devel: Venn's three-self formula, which (with Rufus Anderson's parallel theory) became the standard Protestant goal for mission churches worldwide.
The first African Anglican bishop (Crowther, 1864) and a Yoruba Bible and literature that shaped Yoruba written culture.
Large, self-governing Anglican churches in Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and South India.
Educational institutions such as Fourah Bay College, CMS College Kottayam, King's College Budo and Mengo Hospital.
Linguistic scholarship, including Krapf's Swahili dictionary and grammar.
The East African Revival, a lay renewal movement that spread across East Africa and beyond.
missions/church-missionary-society/outco: CMS was the largest and one of the most influential British missionary societies, and its legacy is above all the Anglican churches of Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya and their neighbours, now among the most vigorous parts of the Anglican Communion. Venn's three-self vision, abandoned in the Niger crisis, was later vindicated by the churches it helped create, and the society continues as the Church Mission Society.

missions/church-missionary-society/count: Sierra Leone
Recaptive villages, Fourah Bay College and the Sierra Leone Native Pastorate (1861), the first self-governing CMS church.
New Zealand
Marsden's mission at Oihi and later Paihia and Waimate; Henry Williams's role in the Treaty of Waitangi; Māori Anglicanism.
India
Agra, Tirunelveli, Travancore, Bengal, the Punjab and Peshawar; CMS churches joined the Church of South India (1947), the Church of North India (1970) and the Church of Pakistan (1970).
Nigeria
Badagry and Abeokuta among the Yoruba, Crowther's Niger Mission from 1857, and the Church of Nigeria, now the largest Anglican province.
Kenya
Krapf and Rebmann at Rabai, Frere Town, and later work among the Kikuyu and Luo; the Anglican Church of Kenya.
Uganda
Mission at the Buganda court, the Uganda Martyrs, the protectorate and the rapid growth of the Church of Uganda.
Canada (Rupert's Land)
Mission among Cree and other First Nations from Red River; Henry Budd ordained 1850; William Duncan's Metlakatla on the Pacific coast (1862).
China
Missions in Ningbo, Hangzhou, Fujian and Sichuan; the Kucheng massacre of 1895.
Japan
Work in Nagasaki, Osaka and Hokkaido, including among the Ainu (John Batchelor); part of the Nippon Sei Ko Kai.
Egypt, Palestine and Iran
Missions in Jerusalem and Nazareth (1851), Isfahan (1869) and Cairo (1882), with schools and hospitals but few converts from Islam.
Pakistan (North-West Frontier)
Peshawar mission and hospitals at Peshawar, Bannu and Quetta (Theodore Pennell at Bannu).
Rwanda and Burundi
The Ruanda Mission (CMS), with Gahini as the cradle of the East African Revival.
Tanzania
Mission stations in central Tanganyika (Mpwapwa) and later the Diocese of Central Tanganyika.
missions/church-missionary-society/journ: Samuel Ajayi Crowther and J. F. Schön with the British Niger Expedition

The government expedition, intended to found a model farm and suppress the slave trade, lost about forty of its roughly 150 Europeans to fever, but Crowther's journals persuaded CMS that Africans must evangelise Africa. He returned to lead the Niger Mission in 1857.
Marsden's first voyage to New Zealand (1814)
Samuel Marsden with Thomas Kendall, William Hall, John King and the Ngāpuhi chief Ruatara
Sailing on the brig Active with Ruatara, who had stayed with him at Parramatta, Marsden preached the first Christian sermon in New Zealand at Oihi on Christmas Day 1814, with Ruatara interpreting.
Krapf and Rebmann in East Africa (1844–1849)
Johann Ludwig Krapf and Johannes Rebmann

Krapf reached Mombasa via Zanzibar in 1844; joined by Rebmann in 1846 he founded Rabai. Rebmann's report of snow on Kilimanjaro (11 May 1848) and Krapf's sighting of Mount Kenya from Kitui (December 1849) were ridiculed in Europe before being confirmed.
The first CMS party to Buganda (1876–1877)
Lt George Shergold Smith, C. T. Wilson, Alexander Mackay and others

Responding to Stanley's appeal, CMS sent eight men in 1876; disease and violence reduced them quickly, but Smith and Wilson crossed Lake Victoria to reach Mutesa's court in June 1877. Smith was killed on Ukerewe island months later; Mackay reached Buganda in 1878.
Bishop Hannington's fatal journey to Buganda (1885)
James Hannington with porters from the coast

Hannington took a new northern route through Maasai country, which the Baganda feared as the 'back door' of invasion. Detained at Lubwa's in Busoga, he was killed with most of his porters on Kabaka Mwanga's orders on 29 October 1885.
missions/church-missionary-society/relat: The treatment of Crowther and African clergy in 1887–91 prompted African-led secessions such as the United Native African Church (1891) and fed the wider African church movement.
CMS leaders played major roles at Edinburgh 1910 and in the International Missionary Council; Max Warren was a key IMC figure.
The Cambridge Seven and student volunteer movements of the 1880s supplied CMS with a wave of university recruits.
missions/church-missionary-society/agree: Venn and the American Board's Rufus Anderson independently formulated the same three-self goal for mission churches.
Shared evangelical theology and anti-slavery commitments, and cooperated in East and Central Africa and India.
missions/church-missionary-society/disag: CMS was founded partly because Anglicans could not accept the LMS's undenominational approach, and the two clashed over Madagascar (1864–74).
CMS resisted African secessions and independent churches and disciplined clergy and members who joined them, even while its own policies had provoked them.
Evangelical Anglicans in India rejected the Lutheran toleration of caste distinctions in church, insisting that converts sit and take communion together.
missions/church-missionary-society/devia: Venn's goal of handing churches to indigenous leaders was abandoned in the 1880s–90s, when European missionaries took over the Niger Mission and appointed white bishops.
A society founded to evangelise became deeply involved in imperial politics, notably in lobbying for Uganda's annexation.
Keswick-influenced missionaries of the 1880s imposed standards of holiness and racial assumptions that departed from Venn's respect for African agency.
